The statement acknowledges a large negative demand-and-supply shock from COVID-19 that will weigh on near-term activity and raise downside risks. The response—cutting the federal funds rate to the effective lower bound (0–0.25 percent), launching large-scale purchases of Treasuries and agency MBS ($500B and $200B at least), and expanding repo, discount window access, and dollar swap lines—aligns with evidence that monetary easing supports real activity by lowering external finance premia and easing credit frictions (Kashyap, Lamont, and Stein, 1994; Gertler and Gilchrist, 1994; Oliner and Rudebusch, 1996). With inflation below target and market-based inflation compensation falling while surveys remain anchored, the stance is consistent with inflation-forecast targeting and credibility considerations that mitigate inflation bias (Svensson; Rogoff) and with the Taylor principle in a severe negative output gap. Given liquidity trap risks, early aggressive balance-sheet actions help prevent deflationary dynamics and stabilize funding markets, including globally via swap lines, consistent with open-economy monetary frameworks and the documented role of financial conditions in propagating shocks. Overall, the near-term outlook remains negative, but decisive policy materially cushions the downside relative to inaction.
